---
title: "Testing the whole tree"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5)
```

`node_test()` asks which clades respond to the environment. Peres-Neto & Kembel (2015)
proposed two frameworks that ask whether phylogenetic composition follows the environment
across the whole tree, and both are in the package. The results below are simulated.

```{r}
library(comdynamite)

set.seed(1)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(20)
traits <- species_traits(tree, lambda = 1, optima_range = c(-1, 101), rmax_range = c(0, 30))
env <- runif(50, 0, 100)
comm <- simulate_static(traits, env, incidence = TRUE)$abundance
keep <- rowSums(comm) > 0
comm <- comm[keep, ]
env <- env[keep]
```

## Phylogenetic community composition

`pcc_test()` takes the principal coordinates of the distances among species, averages them
within sites, and regresses each average on the predictors. The test statistic is the variance
of the adjusted R2 across eigenvectors, and the value to report is the mean of the positive
adjusted R2.

```{r}
pcc <- pcc_test(comm, tree, env, n_perm = 199)
pcc
```

## Phylogenetic beta diversity

`phylo_beta_test()` starts from the distance between communities given by `phylo_beta()`, the
mean phylogenetic distance between their species, and fits a distance-based redundancy
analysis.

```{r}
beta <- phylo_beta_test(comm, tree, env, n_perm = 199)
beta
```

`scores` holds the sites on the principal coordinates of the predicted matrix, which the
authors suggest using to order sites in a heatmap of the community matrix. `plot_phylo_beta()`
draws it, with species in the order of the tree, so that clades replace each other along the
sites when composition follows the environment.

```{r}
plot_phylo_beta(beta, comm, tree)
```

## Principal coordinates of phylogenetic structure

`pcps_test()` computes the principal coordinates of phylogenetic structure (Duarte 2011; Duarte
et al. 2016), the method of the package PCPS (Debastiani & Duarte 2014). By phylogenetic fuzzy
weighting (Pillar & Duarte 2010), each species shares its relative abundance with its relatives,
in proportion to their similarity on the tree, and the principal coordinates of the resulting
matrix order sites by phylogenetic composition. The test covers all the
dissimilarity and, separately, each axis in `axes`, whose `share` is its part of the variation.

```{r}
pcps <- pcps_test(comm, tree, env, n_perm = 199)
pcps
```

Unlike the method of `pcc_test()`, which works on eigenvectors of the tree, this one takes
eigenvectors of the sites, so `scores` can be plotted against the environment. `plot()` draws
the sites on the first two axes, coloured by the environment, with each species as an arrow
from the correlation of its column of the matrix P with the axes.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(pcps)
```

With many species the arrows are hard to read. `clades` draws the species as stars grouped
into clades instead, either the k deepest clades of the tree or groups given by name, such as
families, as in Fig. 1 of Debastiani & Duarte (2014). The plot then shows which lineages go
with which sites.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(pcps, clades = 4, species_labels = FALSE)
```

The package PCPS also draws a curve of phylogenetic signal at the metacommunity level
(`pcps.curve()`), from regressions of community-weighted mean traits on an increasing number of
axes. In simulations by its authors, the curve of traits with low or high phylogenetic signal
did not depart from that expected under Brownian motion (Duarte et al. 2018), so it does not
measure the signal of the trait, and comdynamite does not implement it.

When sites are neighbours and the environment and the communities are both autocorrelated, free
permutations of sites reject far too often. `site_permutations` takes a restricted null model,
such as `torus_permutations()` on a complete grid, in `pcc_test()`, `phylo_beta_test()` and
`pcps_test()` alike. The help of `pcps_test()` gives the rates, including those in a landscape
with edges, where the torus still rejects too often when fields are broad.

## Reading the two p-values

All these functions permute sites, which breaks the link between composition and environment, and
species across the tips, which breaks the link between composition and phylogeny. The association
requires both links, so the p-value to report is `p_max`, the larger of the two. A small
`p_site` with a large `p_species` says that composition follows the environment, but that the
phylogeny adds nothing to it.

The scripts `data-raw/validation_pcc.R` and `data-raw/validation_phylo_beta.R` compare the
rejection rates of these tests with those published.

## Sites that are neighbours

Permutations of sites treat them as exchangeable. When they are neighbours, `site_permutations`
takes a restricted null model, such as those of `torus_permutations()` for a grid on a torus.

Real landscapes have edges, however, and the predictor is often continuous. We compared six nulls
for the site test of `pcps_test()` in `data-raw/validation_continuous_nulls.R`. Communities of 12
species followed a hidden environment, a Gaussian field with exponential covariance, while the
measured predictor was a second, independent field with the same covariance (no relation), or
correlated with the first at 0.6 (power). Landscapes were a 20 x 20 grid, an L-shaped region of
280 random points and a 50 x 8 strip, with ranges of 2, 5 and 10 cells, 200 replicates and 199
null draws each. The nulls were free permutations, the torus (grid only), Moran spectral
randomisation (MSR; Wagner & Dray 2015), an ad hoc rotation and shift of the map wrapped within
its bounding box, a parametric surrogate (a Gaussian field with the range fitted to the predictor
by maximum likelihood, given the observed values by rank) and variogram matching (Viladomat et
al. 2014), in which the predictor is permuted, smoothed over its nearest neighbours and rescaled
so that its variogram matches the observed one.

Rejection rates without a relation (nominal 0.05; with 200 replicates, rates between about 0.02
and 0.08 are compatible with it):

| Landscape | Range | Free | Torus | MSR | Shift and rotate | Parametric | Variogram |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grid | 2 | 0.24 | 0.055 | 0.045 | 0.050 | 0.030 | 0.035 |
| Grid | 5 | 0.60 | 0.100 | 0.075 | 0.085 | 0.055 | 0.055 |
| Grid | 10 | 0.73 | 0.140 | 0.080 | 0.135 | 0.080 | 0.085 |
| L-shape | 2 | 0.27 | | 0.085 | 0.055 | 0.060 | 0.070 |
| L-shape | 5 | 0.49 | | 0.160 | 0.095 | 0.080 | 0.075 |
| L-shape | 10 | 0.65 | | 0.230 | 0.120 | 0.085 | 0.090 |
| Strip | 2 | 0.32 | | 0.025 | 0.055 | 0.035 | 0.025 |
| Strip | 5 | 0.65 | | 0.055 | 0.060 | 0.070 | 0.055 |
| Strip | 10 | 0.79 | | 0.095 | 0.080 | 0.100 | 0.070 |

Free permutations rejected in 24% to 79% of the landscapes. No restricted null stayed at 0.05 in
every case, since all of them became liberal as the range approached the size of the landscape,
when there are few independent patches of environment left to compare. Variogram matching came
closest (mean 0.062, at most 0.09), followed by the parametric surrogate (mean 0.066, at most
0.10). MSR worked on the grid and the strip but not in the L-shaped region (up to 0.23), and the
torus and the rotation were liberal on the grid from a range of 5. Power at a correlation of 0.6
was similar among the restricted nulls (0.90 to 0.94 on average), so the gain in type I error did
not cost power. Variogram matching took about 5 s per test with 199 draws, MSR about 3 s and the
parametric surrogate under 0.5 s. The parametric and variogram surrogates were drawn with
`env_surrogates()`, the code of the package.

The two that came closest are options of the tests, as `null = "variogram"` or
`null = "parametric"` with the coordinates of the sites, and `env_surrogates()` draws them for
other uses, such as null environments for simulations:

```r
pcps_test(comm, tree, env, null = "variogram", coords = coords)
```

With fields as broad as the landscape, p values near 0.05 still deserve caution.

The same surrogates serve as null environments for the simulator. Given a landscape,
`env_surrogates()` returns landscapes with the environment moved but its spatial structure
kept, so a simulated pattern can be compared between the observed landscape and landscapes
where the environment is equally autocorrelated but placed elsewhere:

```r
grid <- landscape_grid(20, torus = FALSE)
nulls <- env_surrogates(grid, n = 99, method = "parametric")
# traits and alpha as in the introductory vignette; here, the decay of similarity with distance
statistic <- function(land) {
  summary_stats(simulate_metacommunity(land, traits, alpha, n_steps = 500))[["decay"]]
}
observed <- statistic(grid)
null <- vapply(nulls, statistic, numeric(1))
```

For an environment that changes in time, `env_surrogates(env_time, coords,
method = "parametric")` moves the whole series of each site to another site, which keeps the
dynamics of each site and changes only their place.

`data-raw/real_data_nulls.R` applies these nulls to the two example data sets, with 999 draws.
For the 314 lakes of `daphniids`, with nine predictors, the relation of phylogenetic
composition to the environment held under every null: `p_site` was 0.001 for the whole
dissimilarity, the first principal coordinate and `phylo_beta_test()`, with free permutations
and with both surrogates. Only the second coordinate changed, from 0.050 with free
permutations and 0.043 with parametric surrogates to 0.123 with the variogram. `p_max` stayed
above 0.1 in every case, as in the analysis of clades, since 13 species give permutations of
species little power. For the 40 ponds of `anurans`, in two cities, the surrogates were drawn
within each city with great-circle distances (`env_surrogates(..., lonlat = TRUE,
strata = city)`, passed to the tests as `null`), and compared with free permutations and with
permutations within each city. No test came below 0.05 under any null (`p_site` 0.09 to 0.70),
so in these ponds the nulls do not change the conclusion.
